det_01.label: Repair Cafe origin: Amsterdam, October 2009
det_01.content: The Repair Cafe movement was founded by Dutch sustainability journalist Martine Postma, who organized the very first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam on 18 October 2009. Postma had become frustrated by the volume of household items being thrown away, and designed Repair Cafes as free, recurring meetings where volunteer fixers help neighbours mend their own broken belongings while sharing skills. The format spread quickly, and on 2 March 2010 Postma incorporated the Repair Cafe International Foundation, which since 2011 has provided manuals, branding and professional support to local groups in the Netherlands and abroad. The dataset analysed in this blog is itself a downstream artefact of that Foundation: it comes from RepairMonitor, the Foundation's data-collection platform that volunteer fixers fill in after each event.

det_02.label: Worldwide growth: ~3,800+ branches in 40+ countries by 2025
det_02.content: From a single Amsterdam meeting in 2009, the network has grown to more than 3,800 active Repair Cafes registered with the Foundation as of October 2025, spread across more than 40 countries. The six largest country networks are the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and the United States. By 2019 there were already roughly 1,700 Repair Cafes in 35 countries; the count crossed 2,000 in 2021 and has nearly doubled since. This rapid international expansion is part of why TidyTuesday picked the dataset for the week of 7 April 2026 — and why the dataset spans dozens of country codes in the `country` column.

det_03.label: RepairMonitor: how this dataset is created
det_03.content: The TidyTuesday CSVs are an export from RepairMonitor, an online tool the Foundation launched so that volunteers at any Repair Cafe can log every visit: the product, the brand, the year of production, the symptom, whether the repair succeeded, and (when it failed) why. RepairMonitor went free-to-access in 2018 to encourage uptake; today its public dashboard offers eight standard visualisations and is the source feeding both this dataset and the Foundation's annual factsheets. Crucially, every row is a self-report by a volunteer at the moment of repair — there is no central QA, which explains the messy free-text fields (`failure_reason_open`, `repair_info_source`) and the missing values that the analyst will have to clean.

det_04.label: Foundation benchmark: 62% success rate in 2024
det_04.content: The Repair Cafe Foundation's 2024 RepairMonitor factsheet reported more than 37,000 repairs logged in that year alone, of which 62 percent were successful — the rest were either unfixable on the spot or only partially repaired. Vacuum cleaners, coffee makers and trousers/pants were the most-brought items in 2024. This 62% benchmark is a useful reference point: any country, brand, or category in our analysis that comes in well above or below it deserves a closer look. The Restart Project's parallel Fixometer (which feeds the Open Repair Alliance dataset of ~130,000 records) reports a similar overall fix rate of around 60%, suggesting the Repair Cafe figure is not an artefact of one platform.

det_05.label: Why repair matters: 62 Mt of e-waste in 2022, rising fast
det_05.content: Repair Cafes exist because the world is drowning in barely-broken stuff. The UN Global E-waste Monitor 2024 found that humans generated a record 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, on track to reach 82 Mt by 2030 — rising 2.6 Mt every year. Less than a quarter (22.3%) was formally collected and recycled, leaving about US$62 billion of recoverable materials in landfill. Each successful Repair Cafe fix is a small subtraction from that flow: roughly 1–3 kg of would-be e-waste avoided, and the embodied carbon of a replacement product saved. This is the climate frame Inside Climate News used when covering the movement in November 2025, and it's the headline reason TidyTuesday chose the dataset.

det_06.label: EU Right to Repair (April 2024) reshapes the policy backdrop
det_06.content: The dataset's later years coincide with a major policy shift: in April 2024 the European Union adopted its Right to Repair Directive, which requires manufacturers to make spare parts available for up to 10 years, to offer repair services beyond the warranty period, and to provide repair information at fair prices. New York State's Digital Fair Repair Act (in force since July 2023) and California's SB 244 (operative since July 2024) carry similar obligations in the US. This matters for our analysis: if the EU directive succeeds, we should eventually see post-2024 country-level differences in success rates, in stated failure reasons (especially `Spare parts not available`), and in repairability scores — particularly between EU member states (NL/BE/DE/FR) and non-EU countries (GB/US). It's still early, but a careful look at year-over-year trends in those failure-reason buckets is worthwhile.

det_07.label: Self-reported repairability is the analyst's most subjective field
det_07.content: The `repairability` column rates how easy a product was to repair on a 1 (difficult) to 10 (easy) scale, but it is filled in by the volunteer fixer at the end of the visit, not by an independent assessor. That makes it a subjective, mood-influenced measure: a product that was successfully repaired will tend to feel 'easy' in retrospect; one that defeated the volunteer feels 'difficult'. The analyst should therefore (a) treat the score as a perception, not a hardware property, (b) check correlation with the binary `repaired` field — strong correlation would be evidence the score mostly tracks outcome, weak correlation would be more interesting — and (c) compare brand- or category-level averages only after filtering for sample size, since one outlier visit can swing a small bucket dramatically.

det_08.label: GenAI vs YouTube as a repair info source — the fresh question
det_08.content: TidyTuesday's prompt explicitly asks whether GenAI is overtaking YouTube as the go-to source of repair information. The dataset's `repair_info_source` and `repair_info_url` free-text fields are where this would show up: volunteers can write 'YouTube', 'ChatGPT', a manufacturer manual URL, a forum thread, etc. ChatGPT was launched in November 2022 and Google Gemini in December 2023, so any signal should appear in 2023+ rows. Given how new these tools are, we should expect YouTube and manufacturer manuals to still dominate — but a non-zero share of GenAI mentions in 2025–2026 would itself be a finding. The analyst will need fuzzy matching (`chatgpt`, `gpt`, `gemini`, `claude`, `ai`, `genai`, `bing chat`) to bucket these reliably.

det_09.label: What makes an item 'unrepairable' — the dominant barriers
det_09.content: Open Repair Alliance and RepairMonitor analyses converge on three main reasons items can't be saved at a community repair event: (1) spare parts are unavailable or prohibitively expensive, (2) the design itself prevents access (glued seams, soldered batteries, proprietary screws), and (3) the volunteers' diagnostic time has run out (a typical session is 1–3 hours per item). These barriers are exactly what the EU and US right-to-repair laws target. The dataset's `failure_reasons` column should therefore show 'Spare parts not available' near the top, alongside 'Design / construction makes repair difficult' and 'Defect not identified'. If the analyst can cross-tabulate these against `kind_of_product`, the result is a near-direct map of where regulation could move the needle.

det_10.label: Carbon impact per repair: a useful interpretive multiplier
det_10.content: The Restart Project estimates that each successful repair of an electric/electronic item at a community session prevents roughly 24 kg of CO2-equivalent emissions on average (the value varies widely by product class — a laptop saves far more than a kettle). If the dataset records N successful repairs of electric/electronic items, multiplying gives a defensible 'CO2 avoided' headline. This is a benchmark the analyst can use to translate raw counts into an environmental statement that resonates with general readers, with the caveat that the multiplier is a class average and undercounts the social/skills externality of the event itself.
